title: Summarize Elements of Effective Security Compliance

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Security compliance means identifying applicable obligations, checking whether required controls are operating, reporting evidence to the correct audience, and understanding the consequences when requirements are not met.
Privacy is part of this work because organizations must recognize which laws apply, who has responsibility for personal data, how long that data is kept, and which rights belong to the individual.
sections.callout: Recognition goal: identify the reporting audience, the type of non-compliance impact, the monitoring method, the applicable privacy scope, and each party's privacy role.

entries.title: Compliance reporting
paragraphs: Communicates evidence, findings, and status regarding required obligations so stakeholders can evaluate whether requirements are being met.

entries.title: Internal reporting
paragraphs: Provides compliance information to organizational stakeholders such as leadership, risk owners, audit teams, and control owners.
entries.recognitionCue: Audience is inside the organization -> internal reporting

entries.title: External reporting
paragraphs: Provides required compliance information to outside parties such as regulators, customers, auditors, or business partners.
entries.recognitionCue: Audience is outside the organization -> external reporting

table.caption: Compliance reporting audiences
rows: Leadership, control owners, internal audit, risk teams

entries.title: Consequences of non-compliance
paragraphs: Outcomes that result when an organization fails to meet legal, regulatory, contractual, or other required obligations.

entries.title: Fines
paragraphs: Monetary penalties imposed for non-compliance.
entries.recognitionCue: Financial penalty paid to an authority -> fine

entries.title: Sanctions
paragraphs: Official restrictions or penalties imposed by an authority. A sanction may restrict activities rather than merely require payment.

entries.title: Reputational damage
paragraphs: Loss of public, customer, partner, or stakeholder trust caused by a compliance failure.
entries.recognitionCue: Loss of trust or public confidence -> reputational damage

entries.title: Loss of license
paragraphs: Revocation or suspension of legal authorization needed to operate or provide a regulated service.
entries.recognitionCue: Authorization to operate is removed -> loss of license

entries.title: Contractual impacts
paragraphs: Consequences arising from unmet agreements, such as breach remedies, termination, service credits, lost opportunities, or restricted partnerships.
entries.recognitionCue: Impact comes from an agreement -> contractual impact

entries.title: Compliance monitoring
paragraphs: Uses ongoing or periodic checks to determine whether required controls and obligations continue to be satisfied.

entries.title: Due diligence/care
paragraphs: Due diligence is reasonable investigation used to understand obligations and risk. Due care is the prudent protective action taken in response.
entries.recognitionCue: Investigate reasonably, then act prudently -> due diligence and due care

entries.title: Attestation and acknowledgement
paragraphs: Formal confirmation that a requirement, statement, or responsibility is understood and that supplied information is accurate.
entries.recognitionCue: Formal confirmation or sign-off -> attestation and acknowledgement

entries.title: Internal and external monitoring
paragraphs: Internal teams review compliance from within the organization, while independent or outside parties provide external review. Both perspectives can contribute evidence.

entries.title: Automation
paragraphs: Uses technology to continuously collect evidence, evaluate configurations, flag exceptions, or report compliance status at scale.
entries.recognitionCue: Technology continuously collects or evaluates evidence -> automation

entries.title: Privacy
paragraphs: Concerns proper handling of personal information and the rights of individuals whose information is collected or used.

entries.title: Legal implications
paragraphs: Privacy obligations are created by the laws and regulations that apply to the organization, the data, the individual, and the processing activity.

entries.title: Local/regional privacy
paragraphs: Privacy requirements imposed below the national level, such as by a state, province, territory, city, or region.
entries.recognitionCue: Requirement comes from a subnational jurisdiction -> local/regional privacy

entries.title: National privacy
paragraphs: Privacy requirements that apply across a country.

entries.title: Global privacy
paragraphs: Privacy obligations spanning multiple countries or jurisdictions. Organizations must determine which requirements apply rather than assuming one rule works everywhere.
entries.recognitionCue: Multiple countries or jurisdictions -> global privacy

entries.title: Data subject
paragraphs: The individual whom personal data identifies or describes.
entries.recognitionCue: The person the personal data is about -> data subject

entries.title: Controller vs. processor
paragraphs: The controller determines why and how personal data is processed. The processor handles personal data on the controller's behalf and according to its instructions.
entries.recognitionCue: Decides purpose and means -> controller; processes for another party -> processor

entries.title: Ownership
paragraphs: Describes accountability and recognized rights associated with data. Specific legal rights and organizational accountability depend on the applicable requirements.

entries.title: Data inventory and retention
paragraphs: A data inventory tracks what personal data exists, where it is stored, and how it is used. Retention rules define how long it is kept and when it should be disposed of.
entries.recognitionCue: Track personal data and keep it only for approved periods -> inventory and retention

entries.title: Right to be forgotten
paragraphs: An individual's right to request deletion of personal data when applicable privacy rules and conditions support that request.
entries.recognitionCue: Individual requests deletion under privacy rules -> right to be forgotten

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Organizational audience = internal reporting; regulator, customer, or other outside audience = external reporting
Money = fine; official restriction = sanction; lost trust = reputational damage
Legal authority to operate is revoked = loss of license; agreement-based consequence = contractual impact
Ongoing obligation checks = compliance monitoring; technology-driven evidence collection = automation
Person described by the data = data subject; decides processing purpose = controller; processes for another = processor
Track what data exists and how long it is kept = data inventory and retention
Applicable deletion request = right to be forgotten

sections.title: Objective 5.4 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Do not confuse the party performing a compliance review with the audience receiving a report. Internal and external monitoring describe who checks compliance; internal and external reporting describe who receives the compliance communication. Also separate the controller, which decides the purpose and means of processing, from the processor, which acts on the controller's behalf.
sections.callout: Identify the clue's function first: monitor, report, penalize, define jurisdiction, assign a privacy role, retain data, or honor an individual right.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Loss of license = authority to operate revoked
Retention = know how long to keep it
Right to be forgotten = applicable deletion request

miniCheck.prompt: A retailer decides why customer purchase histories will be analyzed and which uses are permitted. It hires a cloud analytics provider to process that data only under the retailer's instructions.

fields.label: Party deciding the purpose and permitted use of the data
Party processing the data on another organization's behalf

miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. The retailer is the controller because it determines the purpose and permitted use, while the cloud provider is the processor acting on the retailer's behalf.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Separate the party that decides why and how the data is used from the party that processes it under another organization's instructions.
